# THEORYs with `tags` `personhood`

**Personhood** — what a person is and what makes one persist — personal identity over time, psychological continuity and what matters in survival, persons as bearers of reasons, rights and responsibility. Not the self, which is self (group: philosophy; ADR-024).

| [THEORY-060](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-060.md) v2 | A life story constructed from adolescence on is the form a person's diachronic identity takes, and its content shapes later well-being | McAdams (2019), [LIT-595](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-595.md): narrative identity is "a person's internalized and evolving story of how he or she has become the person he or she is becoming", which gives a life "unity, moral purpose, and temporal coherence". It arrives in adolescence and young adulthood, on the back of autobiographical memory and autobiographical reasoning, as the third layer of a psychological self after the actor of traits and the agent of goals. Stories with agentic and redemptive themes go with well-being and generativity, and in one longitudinal therapy study the story "changes first, and then the storyteller gets better". A review essay: every finding is cited, not shown, and it concedes that having a life story may be a modern cultural construction. Strawson's "Against Narrativity" ([LIT-452](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-452.md)) denies the first half for many people. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-065](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-065.md) | The unity that makes a movement an agent's action is achieved by conformity to the constitutive norms of agency, not given by the causal unity of a mind, so collective agents are agents in the same sense as individual ones | Korsgaard (2014), [LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md): an action is a movement "backed by the agent as a whole", and ordinary attribution implies that the agent was active and that the action expresses who she is. Following the categorical and hypothetical imperatives gives action the form of self-determined efficacy; the content of the maxims chosen under that form constitutes practical identity. Self-consciousness of one's own attitudes breaks the unity an animal is given, and reason is the work of rebuilding it, so unity of agency "is an achievement, not a given", and people can act together "in the most literal sense". The Tanner Lectures ([LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md)) supply the reflective structure the chapter assumes. Argued, with the Kantian premise assumed and the collective mechanism stated in a paragraph. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-075](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-075.md) | Obligation is the reflective rejection of what would violate the agent's practical identity, and moral obligation follows only because valuing any practical identity commits the agent to valuing her humanity | Korsgaard (1992), [LIT-564](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-564.md): because human consciousness is reflective, an agent must act on reasons, and so must identify with some law, a "practical identity": "a description under which you value yourself". "Your reasons express your identity, your nature; your obligations spring from what that identity forbids." Obligation is "the reflective rejection of a threat to your identity", unconditional where violation would be worse than death. Identities are a "jumble" and differ across social worlds, so this much yields no morality. Moral obligation enters because valuing any identity requires valuing one's humanity, the source of all one's reasons. "The Normative Constitution of Agency" ([LIT-587](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-587.md)) later makes practical identity the content of maxims chosen under the formal norms. Argued, with the key steps flagged by their author as sketchy; the commentaries and reply are unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-076](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-076.md) | Diachronic self-governance is constituted by cross-temporal links of intention that are intrapersonal analogues of shared intention, not by narrative unity and not by intertemporal bargaining | Bratman (2018), [LIT-567](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-567.md): an agent governs herself over time when she is self-governing at each time along a planned activity and her intentions at those times interlock as the intentions of people acting together do, so that she acts "together" with herself. Her standpoints include a conditional, reflexive end of her own diachronic self-governance, which is what lets resolve against temptation be self-governed while following through on Kavka's toxin is not. He rejects the bargaining model (McClennen, Ainslie) in two sentences and calls narrative unity less basic in one. A philosophical model argued from cases; the analogy is partial by its author's account and its terms come from a book the record has not read. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-120](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-120.md) v2 | A motive is the agent's own, and she acts of her own free will, when she identifies with it, and that is all the freedom moral responsibility requires: identification is the conformity of the effective desire to a decisive higher-order volition (1971), and later wholehearted acceptance with no conflict at any higher order | Frankfurt's hierarchical, or endorsement, account, from his own texts: the 1971 paper ([LIT-692](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-692.md), read) and the 2004 Tanner Lectures ([LIT-293](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-293.md), read). A person's will is the desire that moves him to act; he identifies with a desire by wanting it to be his will, decisively, and he acts of his own free will when the will that moves him is the will he wants. In 2004 the condition is "volitional unanimity" with no conflict "at any higher order", and identification is "willing acceptance", which may be resigned. Acting of one's own free will is what responsibility requires, and alternatives and history are irrelevant. The 1987 and 1992 revisions are held only by report. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-131](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-131.md) v2 | A corporation whose Corporate Internal Decision (CID) Structure, an organizational chart of stations plus recognition rules embedded in corporate policy, licenses redescribing its members' acts as done for corporate reasons is a non-eliminable intentional agent, unlike a mob; and if intentional agency suffices for moral personhood, which French asserts but here says he cannot further argue, such a corporation is a full-fledged moral person | French (1979), [LIT-727](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-727.md). Moral persons are non-eliminable subjects of accountability, so intentional agents. A corporation's CID Structure licenses redescribing members' acts as corporate acts, and an act that implements established corporate policy is done for corporate reasons. Proposed: the step from agency to moral personhood is asserted, and corporate intentionality is shown by licensed redescription, not by any test. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-417](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-417.md) | 'Personal identity' names several largely independent questions, among them who one is (characterization), what a person is, what it takes for one to persist, how many of us there are and what matters in survival; the persistence question concerns numerical identity, which 'remaining the same person' in the characterization sense presupposes, and posing it as 'a person at one time and a person at another' assumes that we are persons essentially | Olson (2002; rev. 2023), [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md), read in [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md). Seven questions: characterization, personhood, persistence, evidence, population, personal ontology and what matters. The distinctions are conceptual and the record holds them as stated. They do not say which answer to any of the questions is right; the entry's own answer, animalism, is argued in other sections and is not part of this account. The self is set aside by the entry, so the map does not cover the self literature. | Active |
| [THEORY-447](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-447.md) v2 | Granted that a person survives a brain transplant and that half a brain would do, each product of a division stands in all that matters in ordinary survival, so what matters is not identity, which is one-one and all-or-nothing, but psychological relations that can branch and come in degrees | Parfit (1971), [LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md), read in [NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md), with the fission dilemma as Olson's survey states it, [LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md) ([NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)). The division argument is strong given its premises, and the premises are stated: brain-transplant survival is assumed, not argued. It does not say that connectedness matters more than continuity, which Parfit asserts for lack of space, or that a copy or a transcript is a survivor: the dependence q-memory needs is left "(whatever that is)". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-464](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-464.md) v2 | In the ethical questions that seem to turn on whether someone is the same person, among them prudential concern, responsibility, abortion, advance directives and the separateness of persons, the relation that decides is usually not numerical identity but one that comes apart from it, so the metaphysics of persistence constrains these questions and rarely settles them | Dufner (2025), [LIT-130](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-130.md), the SEP entry that replaced Shoemaker's, read in [NOTE-166](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-166.md). A survey that takes no side; the account is the reading's synthesis of what it reports, correcting a seeded summary that said the metaphysics "jointly settle" the ethics. It does not say identity never matters: uniqueness may matter for positional goods, and biological views support prohibiting abortion more strongly than psychological ones, without forcing it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-476](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-476.md) | If continuant persons are maximal aggregates of person-stages interrelated by the psychological relation R, then the relation of belonging to one person is R itself, so Parfit's premises do not show that identity is not what matters; the price is that persons overlap in fission and are counted by a relation weaker than identity | Lewis (1976), [LIT-446](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-446.md), read in [NOTE-373](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-373.md). Shown: that identity being one-one and all-or-nothing, and what matters branching and coming in degrees, do not entail that identity is not what matters, once stages and continuants are told apart; and that under supervaluation degrees of I-relatedness equal degrees of R-relatedness. Stipulated: that persons are the maximal R-interrelated aggregates. Conceded as costly: counting persons by tensed identity, which "is not a kind of identity". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-531](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-531.md) v2 | Told in the third person, a transfer of memories and character between two bodies reads as the persons exchanging bodies; told in the first person, no predicted psychological change removes the subject's reason to fear pain to his own body, and the step that completes the exchange happens only to the other man, so the two tellings support opposite criteria | Williams (1970), [LIT-462](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-462.md), read in [NOTE-387](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-387.md). The strongest step is shown given its premise: the last step of the series that turns amnesia into a body exchange changes nothing for the subject. The premise, that psychological change cannot remove the reason to fear pain, is argued from cases. Williams claims no criterion of identity, calls his resolution "rather shaky" and "risky", and does not treat fission. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-546](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-546.md) v2 | A person persists by psychological continuity, not by sameness of substance or of the human animal; Locke's sameness of consciousness, which he leaves undefined, meets the charges of circularity, intransitivity and gaps when recast as overlapping chains of causally dependent psychological states with quasi-memory, and fission then needs either a clause against branching or multiple occupancy | Locke (1694), [LIT-464](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-464.md), read in [NOTE-385](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-385.md), with the repairs as Olson's survey ([LIT-454](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-454.md), [NOTE-374](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-374.md)) and Parfit ([LIT-447](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-447.md), [NOTE-378](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-378.md)) give them. Locke shows that same man, same substance and same person can be given different conditions; that the person's are those of consciousness he asserts and illustrates. The repaired criterion is the majority view in the survey, and its author, an animalist, argues it implies two thinkers in every chair. It is a criterion of persistence, not an account of what matters or of what we are made of. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-590](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-590.md) | The self whose governance makes action autonomous is not the self whose persistence is personal identity: governance by an essence of volitional necessities would make action authentic, not autonomous; losing a defining care costs one's grasp of who one is, not one's existence; and wholeheartedness won by extruding a desire is a defence, not health | Velleman (2002), [LIT-292](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-292.md), read in [NOTE-268](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-268.md). A critique of Frankfurt's late (1990s) view that autonomy is governance by the essential character of the will, an essence that is also the condition of one's identity. It argues by counterexample (Winnicott's False Self, the Agamemnon sequel), from Freud's Rat Man, and by debunking genealogy. The positive view, that "self" marks reflexivity and that autonomous action is motivated in part by the understanding, is stated "briefly" and argued elsewhere. Frankfurt's reply is unread. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-650.md) | Whether a self at one time is the same as a self at another has an answer only relative to a level of abstraction fixed by the purpose of asking, and asked at no such level it has none; the question with a substantive answer is what makes a self one thing at a time | Floridi (2011), [LIT-136](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-136.md), read in [NOTE-130](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-130.md). The deflation of diachronic identity is an informal argument from examples that rests on the method of levels of abstraction, assumed from elsewhere; that this "is not relativism" is one sentence, and that individuation comes before identification is asserted. It is not, as its title suggests, a criterion of personal identity, and its positive answer to the synchronic question, the three-membranes model, is "somewhat figurative" by its author's word. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-681](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-681.md) | If every real idea derives from an impression, there is no idea of a simple self persisting through life; the mind is a bundle of perceptions, and the identity ascribed to it is produced by the imagination passing easily along resemblance and causation, as with a rebuilt ship or a growing oak, though Hume's Appendix concedes that this does not explain what unites the perceptions | Hume (1739, with the Appendix of 1740), [LIT-451](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-451.md), read in [NOTE-386](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-386.md). The negative half is as strong as the copy principle. The mechanism of the fiction is argued by analogy from cases of usage. The account of what unites the bundle is withdrawn by its author, who names the two principles he cannot reconcile. It does not say there is no self in any sense, and it leaves identity "as it regards our passions" to Book 2. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1565](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1565.md) v2 | Luper argues that Epicurus's case that death is nothing to us needs intrinsic hedonism and a narrow view of extrinsic harm, that without them death can harm by depriving one of goods, and reports Pitcher's preferentialist view that posthumous events harm the living person by thwarting desires held while alive, a view the entry shows contested | Luper, SEP "Death" (revised 2026), [LIT-1792](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1792.md), read in [NOTE-1294](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1294.md) in place of Pitcher (1984, [LIT-1740](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1740.md)), which the entry gives in two paragraphs. It also defends a compositional account of life and the loss-of-life account of death, rejects subsequentism, and sides with Williams's critics on immortality. | Active |
| [THEORY-1572](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1572.md) v2 | Johnston withdraws the account of his Surviving Death, on which our deepest future-directed attitudes fix which future embodiments are ours, arguing that every reductionist account of personal identity breeds fellow travelers with moral status, and holds instead that we are essentially embodied wills whose present embodiments are not essential | Johnston (2023), [LIT-1788](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1788.md), read in [NOTE-1257](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1257.md) in place of Surviving Death ([LIT-1759](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1759.md)). The book's surrogate for the resurrection hope, living on "in the onward rush of humankind" as a self fixed by future-directed attitudes, is given up because reductionist selves multiply bearers of moral status. Programmatic: many arguments are deferred to other papers, and theism carries the account of where wills come from. | Active |
| [THEORY-1609](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1609.md) v2 | Hershfield reviews evidence, mostly from his own studies, that people who feel less similar to their future selves treat them more like strangers and choose less patiently, while directly reported liking and caring for the future self, answered near ceiling, did not predict choice | Hershfield (2011), [LIT-1702](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-1702.md), read in [NOTE-1259](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1259.md) from the accepted manuscript. Following Parfit, future self-continuity has three proposed components, similarity, vividness and positivity, each measured or manipulated in studies of saving and discounting. Apart from one r = .47, the review gives no effect sizes. It suggests, untested, that late in life the future self may continue in one's offspring. | Active |
| [THEORY-1610](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1610.md) v2 | Parfit argues that narrow person-affecting principles fail in non-identity and different-number cases, and that a wide person-affecting principle, on which being caused to exist with a life worth living is an intrinsic benefit and an outcome is in one way worse if it benefits people less, solves the non-identity problem and keeps the relation of being better transitive | Parfit's last paper (2017), read in full and unfinished by the editor's note ([NOTE-1263](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1263.md)). It keeps the No Difference View, retracts his 1984 appeal to an impersonal principle, and offers a person-affecting one in its place. Benefits to future people are owed to whoever will exist, which our choices decide. | Active |
| [THEORY-1650](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1650.md) | Dranseika, granting Devanesan that a mereology of pregnancy shapes which analogies an argument about abortion can use without fixing its conclusion, argues that the dependence also runs the other way: normative commitments may legitimately guide the choice among mereological views still in contention, but a mereology chosen partly to fit a commitment gives that commitment no independent support | Mereological implications of the ethics of pregnancy (Dranseika, J Med Ethics 2026), read in [NOTE-1751](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1751.md) (Read), standing in for [LIT-2409](../../../record/literature.d/LIT-2409.md). Dranseika accepts Devanesan's thesis that a mereology of pregnancy changes the route to an ethical conclusion without entailing it, and adds the converse: normative commitments can legitimately shape which mereology one adopts, but a mereology chosen to fit a commitment is then no independent evidence for it. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1657](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1657.md) | Millum argues that there is no distinctive right to an open future: the argument from future autonomy fails because autonomy as demand is grounded in a present capacity young children lack, the argument from analogy explains its clear cases by bodily integrity and harm, and the positive version is only children's interests, which give future options no priority over their other interests; so citing the right decides nothing and obscures the weighing that does. | Millum (2025), read in [NOTE-1734](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1734.md) (Read). Millum argues that there is no distinctive "right to an open future" (Feinberg's rights-in-trust). As a negative right it would rest either on future autonomy or on analogy. | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1671](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1671.md) | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity (2024) argues that clinicians may perform nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery on a prepubescent child, of any sex characteristics, only when it is medically necessary in a strict sense, a serious and time-sensitive threat to physical health with no less invasive or postponable alternative, because what grounds the consensus protecting girls is not a benefit–risk judgment by others but the child's right, held in trust, to make intimate decisions about their own sexual anatomy later, and that right does not vary with sex. | The Brussels Collaboration on Bodily Integrity, read in [NOTE-1799](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1799.md) (Skimmed). Restricting itself to nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery by licensed clinicians on prepubescent children in Global North healthcare systems, and taking no position on criminal law or religious practice outside healthcare, the collaboration argues: there is a near-universal consensus that clinicians may not perform any medically unnecessary genital procedure on endosex girls, however minimal; the sound reasons for that consensus are not benefit–risk calculations but respect for privacy, bodily integrity, developing sexual boundaries and future genital autonomy; those reasons apply equally to intersex children and endosex boys; so clinicians should perform no nonvoluntary genital cutting or surgery on any child unless it is medically necessary in a strict sense (a serious, time-sensitive threat to physical health, no less invasive or postponable alternative, preserving future choice). They reject the "mental health" defence of early surgery, hold that errors of commission and omission are not symmetric, and invoke Feinberg's "right in trust". | Proposed |
| [THEORY-1686](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1686.md) | Nix argues that because Canadian law treats MAID as a medical intervention whose provision the duty of care permits only while the patient is suffering intolerably, and conceives that suffering as intolerable to the patient herself, an advance request for MAID by a person with dementia cannot be operationalized either by pre-specified impairments, which people cannot forecast, or by pre-specified behaviours, which an outside observer cannot read as subjective intolerability, unless an objective conception of suffering is adopted and validated scales are built. | Nix (2024), Operationalizing the Intolerable Suffering Criterion in Advance Requests for MAID for People Living with Dementia in Canada, read in [NOTE-1731](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1731.md) (Read). | [THEORY-1696](../../../record/theory.d/THEORY-1696.md) | Harman's survey treats the moral question whether abortion is wrong apart from whether it should be legally restricted, and organises the debate as arguments against abortion with replies. Among the replies read: Thomson's violinist case grants the fetus a right to life and denies that this makes abortion wrong, recasting abortion as withdrawing life-sustaining aid; and McMahan's time-relative interests view denies that a pre-conscious fetus has an interest in its future, because it has no psychological connection to it | The Ethics of Abortion (Harman, Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy, 2025), read in [NOTE-1788](../../../record/notes.d/NOTE-1788.md) (Skimmed). The entry asks one question: "is abortion morally wrong?" It sets aside whether abortion should be legally restricted as "an open and further question".
